Our scheduling app now syncs with Outlook.

It took four months. Two engineers.

If you've ever double-booked yourself because your calendar lived in one place and your bookings lived in another, this one's for you.

If you've tried to book a meeting from a scheduling tool and got a conflict because someone's Outlook calendar wasn't checked, you know why this mattered. Now availability pulls from Outlook directly, so the times you see are the times you're actually free.

The hard part was keeping it accurate. Outlook calendars change constantly: recurring events get moved, people decline invites, time zones shift. We spent most of those four months on edge cases like those, not on the connection itself.

Thanks to the two engineers who stuck with it. It's live for everyone now.

If you use Outlook and schedule meetings, try it and tell us what breaks.

Most small teams start building before they agree on what they are building. Someone has an idea, a few people sketch it on a whiteboard, and within a week there is code. That feels fast. Then, a month in, two people discover they were solving different problems, or one person has built the account settings around an assumption the other never shared. Nobody did anything wrong. The decision just lived in three heads, and nobody wrote it down.

A design doc is the cheapest fix for that. It is a short document, often a few pages, that says what the thing is for, what it will and will not do, and how it will work at a high level. You write it before the first real line of code, you share it with the people who will build it, and you let them argue with it. The argument is the point. It is far cheaper to discover a disagreement in a paragraph than in a pull request, and far cheaper again than in a customer's complaint.

Every small team has lived through the same moment. Two engineers spend three weeks building a feature, open the pull request, and discover they understood the problem differently. One pictured a settings page, the other a wizard. Neither was wrong about the code. They were wrong about what they were building together, and nobody had written it down in a form the other could check. The fix that follows is usually a rewrite, a tense meeting, and a quiet resolution to "be more aligned next time."

A design doc is a short, written answer to a few simple questions before anyone starts coding: what problem are we solving, what are we proposing, what alternatives did we consider, and what could go wrong. It doesn't need to be formal or long. Often it runs two or three pages. But the act of writing it forces the fuzzy idea in your head into sentences that someone else can question. For small teams, where there is no architecture review board or project manager to catch misunderstandings, that single step can save weeks of work and a good deal of frustration.

cells.source:
Most small teams skip design docs. The reasoning usually goes something like this: we're five people, we talk all day, we can just start building and sort things out as we go. And for a while, that works. Everyone holds the whole system in their head, decisions get made in hallway conversations, and the code itself becomes the record of what was decided. Then the team doubles, or someone leaves, or a feature turns out to touch three services nobody expected, and suddenly nobody can remember why the auth layer works the way it does or which of the two competing approaches was rejected and for what reason. The cost of skipping the design phase doesn't show up on day one. It shows up months later, quietly, as rework, as arguments that repeat themselves, and as new engineers who have to reverse-engineer intent from code.

A design doc is not a bureaucratic ritual, and it doesn't have to be a forty-page document that gets approved by a committee. At its best, it's a short, written argument: here is the problem, here is what we're going to do about it, here are the alternatives we considered, and here is why we chose this path over the others. Writing that down forces a kind of clarity that's hard to reach through conversation alone. Vague assumptions become explicit, and explicit assumptions can be challenged before they're expensive to fix. A two-page doc that a colleague reads in twenty minutes can surface a flaw that would have cost two weeks of coding. For small teams, where every engineer's time is a large fraction of total capacity, that trade is especially good.

The nightly job failed with an access denied error on `s3:PutObject`. Someone changed the S3 bucket policy, and the job's role no longer has that permission. The job isn't broken, and nothing in the code changed.

To confirm, check the current bucket policy and the role's effective permissions:

```bash
aws s3api get-bucket-policy --bucket <bucket> --query Policy --output text

aws iam simulate-principal-policy \
  --policy-source-arn <role-arn> \
  --action-names s3:PutObject \
  --resource-arns arn:aws:s3:::<bucket>/*
```

If the simulation says `implicitDeny` or `explicitDeny`, look for a Deny statement in the bucket policy or a permissions boundary on the role. An explicit Deny overrides any Allow.

To find out who made the change and when, search CloudTrail:

```bash
aws cloudtrail lookup-events \
  --lookup-attributes AttributeKey=EventName,AttributeValue=PutBucketPolicy \
  --max-results 20
```

Then decide what to do:

- If the change was unintended, restore the previous policy or add a statement that allows `s3:PutObject` for the job's role on the bucket prefix it writes to. Scope it to that prefix rather than the whole bucket.
- If the change was intended, the job's role needs the permission added to its own policy, or the job needs a different role. Get the owner of the bucket policy to agree before editing either one.

After the fix, re-run the failed job manually to confirm the write succeeds, and don't wait for the next nightly run to find out.

To confirm, check the failing run's logs for the `AccessDenied` error and the role ARN in the assumed-role session. Then pull the current policy and the role's effective permissions:

```bash
aws s3api get-bucket-policy --bucket <bucket> --query Policy --output text | jq .
aws iam simulate-principal-policy \
  --policy-source-arn <job-role-arn> \
  --action-names s3:PutObject \
  --resource-arns "arn:aws:s3:::<bucket>/<prefix>/*"
```

If the simulation says `implicitDeny` or `explicitDeny`, the bucket policy is the cause.   "Sid": "NightlyJobPutObject",
```json
  "Effect": "Allow",
  "Principal": { "AWS": "<job-role-arn>" },
  "Action": "s3:PutObject",
  "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::<bucket>/<prefix>/*"
}
```

Scope the grant to the prefix and action the job needs. Don't widen it to `s3:*` or `Resource: *` to get the job running. If the policy is managed in Terraform or CloudFormation, make the change there so the next apply doesn't revert it.
